headline: The Kennedy Center closed for its roof. It had the money.
summary: The Kennedy Center in Washington shut this month, citing a failing roof canopy and a partial ceiling collapse. Former employees told Congress that its boss, Matt Floca, had repair money from a $257 million earmark and halted the plan in April. Floca says a quote came in at triple the estimate, so he folded the work into a bigger one.

cover_question.q: Who decides a building is unsafe?

cover_answer: Its bosses did. Ex-staff say they knew a year ago.
table_question: If you had money to fix a leak, is waiting for a better plan okay?

5-7.script: A famous theater in Washington closed because its roof leaks and a piece of ceiling fell down. People who used to work there say the bosses had the money to fix it a year ago and didn't. It's like knowing your bike tire is flat, owning a pump, and leaving it in the garage. The grown-ups are sorting out who was right.
5-7.why: A flat tire and a pump in the garage. They know exactly what that feels like. The argument in Congress is noise to them; the pump is the story.
5-7.why_long: A six-year-old reasons from what is in front of them, so the script swaps a $257 million earmark for a pump left in the garage while the tire sits flat. That is the whole allegation at a size they can hold. Expect "did anyone get hurt?" The article doesn't say anyone was. The doors shut before the show, and they stay shut for now.

8-12.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
8-12.script: Congress gave the Kennedy Center $257 million in 2025 to fix its leaking roof. In April the boss paused the plan over a quote at triple the estimate. In September a ceiling gave way and the doors shut. Like putting off a homework fix, and the deadline lands first.
8-12.why: One chain, money to plan to pause to collapse. Where did it break?
8-12.why_long: This age is working out chains of cause and effect, so the script hands them the chain, money to plan to pause to collapse, and lets them say which link broke. Expect "so was the boss lying?" Not proven. He says the work changed shape, not that it stopped. The ex-staff say it stopped. Congress is asking.

13-17.script: A repair quote comes in at triple the estimate. Re-plan, or fix the leak now? The Kennedy Center re-planned; the ceiling gave way. Second: the whistleblowers are anonymous and the senator chasing it is a Democrat after a Trump-run board. Trust the letter?
13-17.why: A management call, then a question about who is telling the story.
13-17.why_long: A teenager can hold two true things at once, so the script gives them the pair: a boss who may have made a sensible call on cost, and a building that fell in anyway. Then it asks them to weigh the source, anonymous staff and a partisan senator: argument practised, Kuhn's term. Expect "so who's right?" Unknown. A status report was due Friday.

5-7.a: The bosses say it is closed while they fix it. The article doesn't say when it opens, so nobody has a date yet.

8-12.q: Why didn't they just fix the roof?
8-12.a: The boss says the quote cost triple what he expected, so he folded it into a bigger plan. The ex-staff say he simply stopped.

8-12.q: Where did the money come from?
8-12.a: Congress set aside $257 million for it in the 2025 tax and spending bill. The whistleblowers say it was in hand.

13-17.q: Who decides a building is unsafe?
13-17.a: Its bosses did. Floca says a summer inspection found damage spreading in the roof. Ex-staff say the risks were known a year ago.

13-17.q: Why does Trump care about a theater?
13-17.a: He put his people on its board and his name on the building. A judge ordered the name off; hours later the board closed it.
